text: Joab son of Zeruiah could tell that the king's heart longed for Absalom.

So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought back a wise woman from there. He told her, pretend to be in mourning; put on mourning clothes, don't use any oil, and act like a woman who has been grieving for the dead for a long time.
Then go to the king and speak to him the way I tell you. And Joab put the words in her mouth.
When the woman from Tekoa came before the king, she fell facedown on the ground to pay him honor and said, help me, Your Majesty!
The king asked her, what's troubling you? She answered, I am indeed a widow; my husband has died.
Your servant had two sons; they were fighting out in a field with no one there to separate them, and one of them struck the other and killed him.

Now the whole family has risen up against your servant, saying, hand over the one who struck down his brother, so we can put him to death for the life of the brother he killed, even if it means destroying the heir. This way they would put out the last burning coal I have left, leaving my husband no name or descendant on the earth.
The king told the woman, go home; I will issue an order on your behalf.
But the woman of Tekoa said to the king, my lord the king, let the guilt fall on me and on my father's family, and let the king and his throne be free of blame.
The king said, if anyone says anything more to you about this, bring them to me, and they will never bother you again.

She said, please, may the king invoke the name of the LORD your God, so that the avenger of blood does not bring even more destruction and my son is not destroyed. He said, as surely as the LORD lives, not one hair of your son will fall to the ground.
Then the woman said, please let your servant say one more thing to my lord the king. Speak, he said.
The woman said, why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? By saying this, doesn't the king convict himself, since he has not brought his own banished son back home?

We will all die eventually; we are like water spilled on the ground, which can't be gathered up again. But God does not just take away life — he finds ways so that a banished person is not permanently cut off from him.
Now the reason I have come to say this to my lord the king is that the people have frightened me, and your servant thought, I will speak to the king; maybe he will grant his servant's request.
Perhaps the king will listen and rescue his servant from the hand of the man trying to cut off both me and my son from the inheritance God gave us.
Your servant thought, may the word of my lord the king bring me peace, for my lord the king is like an angel of God in discerning good from evil. May the LORD your God be with you.
Then the king said to the woman, don't hide from me the answer to what I am going to ask you. Let my lord the king speak, she said.

The king asked, is Joab's hand behind all of this? The woman answered, as surely as you live, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right or the left from anything my lord the king says. Yes, it was your servant Joab who told me to do this and put these very words in my mouth.
Your servant Joab did this to turn the situation around. But my lord has wisdom like that of an angel of God, and knows everything that happens in the land.
The king said to Joab, very well, I will do it. Go and bring back the young man Absalom.

Joab fell facedown on the ground to honor the king and blessed him. Joab said, today your servant knows he has found favor with you, my lord the king, because the king has granted his servant's request.
So Joab went to Geshur and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.
But the king said, he must go to his own house; he is not to come into my presence. So Absalom went to his own house and did not see the king's face.
In all Israel there was no man so highly praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom; from the top of his head to the sole of his foot he had no flaw.
Whenever he cut the hair of his head, which he did once a year because it grew too heavy for him, he would weigh it, and it came to two hundred shekels by the royal standard.
Three sons were born to Absalom, and one daughter, named Tamar, who grew up to be a beautiful woman.
Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem without ever seeing the king's face.
Then Absalom sent for Joab to send him to the king, but Joab refused to come to him; he sent for him a second time, but Joab still refused to come.
So Absalom told his servants, look, Joab's field is right next to mine, and he has barley growing there; go set it on fire. So Absalom's servants set the field ablaze.
Then Joab went to Absalom's house and demanded, why have your servants set my field on fire?

Absalom answered Joab, look, I sent for you and told you to come here so I could send you to the king to ask, why did I ever come back from Geshur? It would be better for me if I were still there. Now then, let me see the king's face, and if I am guilty of anything, let him put me to death.
So Joab went to the king and reported this to him. Then the king summoned Absalom, who came in and bowed facedown to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.
